unit.title: Use strategies to identify job opportunities

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain how to assess your own skills, interests and values before looking for a job in hospitality, and why this helps.
essays.modelAnswer: Before looking for work, I would take time to understand myself. First, I list my skills. Some are technical skills from my training, such as making beds to standard, cleaning a bathroom, using a floor machine or setting a table. Others are transferable skills, such as communication, teamwork, punctuality, problem solving and staying calm with guests, which are useful in every job. I can ask my instructor and classmates what they think I do well. Next, I think about my interests: do I enjoy working with people at the front desk, or do I prefer working behind the scenes in housekeeping or the kitchen? Then I think about my values and needs, such as the pay I need, whether I can work shifts and weekends, how far I can travel, and whether I want to work overseas. I also note the skills I still need to build. Knowing all this helps me choose jobs that suit me, explain my strengths in my CV and at interview, and plan any extra training I need.
markingPoints: Lists technical skills from training, with examples
Lists transferable skills, with examples, and asks others for their views
Considers interests (front of house or behind the scenes)
Considers values and needs (pay, shifts, travel, overseas) and skills still to build
Explains why it helps: choosing suitable jobs, the CV and interview, and a training plan

essays.stem: Describe at least five different sources of job opportunities for a trained hospitality worker in Jamaica, and say how to use each one.
essays.modelAnswer: There are many places to find hotel and villa jobs. Job adverts appear in newspapers and on online job sites; I should check them often and apply before the closing date. Many hotels, resort groups and villa companies post vacancies on their own websites and social media pages, so I can follow the ones I would like to work for. The Centre's career or job placement office, and the HEART/NSTA Trust, share openings and help with CVs and interviews. Government employment services, through the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, list local jobs and run approved overseas work programmes. Licensed recruitment agencies match workers with employers; I should check that an agency is licensed, and never pay to be given a job. Job fairs and recruitment days let me meet many employers in one day, so I take copies of my CV and dress smartly. Telling family, friends, instructors and former co-workers that I am looking helps me hear about jobs that are never advertised. I can also send my CV with a short letter to properties I would like to work for, even if they have not advertised.
markingPoints: Job adverts in newspapers and on online job sites, used correctly
Employers' own websites and social media pages
The Centre's career office, the HEART/NSTA Trust and government employment services
Licensed recruitment agencies and job fairs, used safely
Contacts, and sending a CV to properties that have not advertised

essays.stem: Explain how a trainee can use family, friends, instructors and people they meet to find out about jobs that are not advertised, and how to do this politely.
essays.modelAnswer: Many jobs, especially in small villas and guest houses, are filled by word of mouth before they are ever advertised, so the people I know can help me find work. I would tell family, friends, neighbours, church members, my instructors and the people I met on work experience that I have finished my training, and what kind of job I want. I would ask them to tell me if they hear of an opening and, if they work in a hotel, whether they could pass on my CV. At Centre open days, job fairs and community events, I would introduce myself politely to hotel staff and managers, say what I am trained in, ask about work there, and take their contact details. I could ask someone who does a job I want, such as a butler, if I can talk to them about what the work is like. I would always be polite, thank people for their help, keep in touch without pestering them, and keep my social media respectful, because contacts may look at it. In return, I would help others when I can.
markingPoints: Explains that many jobs are filled through contacts before they are advertised
Tells family, friends, instructors and work-experience contacts what job they want
Asks contacts to share openings and pass on the CV
Introduces self politely at events, and asks people who do a job what it is like
Is polite, thanks people, keeps in touch without pestering, and keeps social media respectful

essays.stem: Describe how to read a job advert carefully and decide whether to apply. Use the example of a hotel job advert.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the whole advert slowly, more than once. First I look at the job title, the employer and where the job is. Then I read the duties, to see what the work involves day to day. Next I check the requirements, and I separate the essential ones, which I must have, from the desirable ones, which are a plus. For example, an advert for a room attendant at a hotel in Ocho Rios might ask for NVQ-J Level 2 in housekeeping and a Food Handler's Permit as essential, and experience and a second language as desirable. I would check the hours and shifts, the pay if it is given, and the closing date. Then I read how to apply, by email, online form or in person, and what to send, such as a CV, a cover letter and copies of certificates. I would apply if I have all the essential requirements, or nearly all and can explain how I will get them soon. In my application, I would show how my skills match the duties and requirements in the advert.
markingPoints: Reads the whole advert carefully: job title, employer and location
Reads the duties
Separates essential from desirable requirements, with an example
Checks the hours, pay, closing date and how to apply
Applies if the essential requirements are met, and matches skills to the advert

essays.stem: Describe the career pathway in one hotel department (housekeeping, kitchen or front office), from an entry-level job to a senior job, and explain how a worker can move up.
essays.modelAnswer: In housekeeping, a worker usually starts as a room attendant, or as a public area or laundry attendant, cleaning rooms and areas to the hotel's standard. With experience and good work, the next step is often senior room attendant or floor supervisor, who checks rooms, trains new staff and plans the work for a floor. After that come housekeeping supervisor and then assistant executive housekeeper, who helps to manage staff rosters, stock and budgets. The senior job is the executive housekeeper, who manages the whole department and works with the other heads of department. In a villa, a housekeeper may become the villa manager. To move up, a worker should do excellent, reliable work, be on time, keep a good attitude, learn every task in the department and ask for more responsibility. They should take further training, such as NVQ-J Level 3, supervision courses and computer skills, and learn a second language if they can. They should tell their supervisor about their goals, and apply for promotions when they come up.
markingPoints: A correct entry-level job for the chosen department
At least two correct steps in the middle of the pathway
A correct senior job for the department
Moves up through excellent, reliable work and taking on responsibility
Further training (such as Level 3, supervision or a language), and telling the supervisor about goals

essays.stem: Explain how to recognise and avoid job scams, including offers of work overseas.
essays.modelAnswer: Job scams try to take a job seeker's money or personal details. Warning signs include: being asked to pay a fee for a job, a visa or training before you are hired; pay that seems far too high for the work; a job offered without any interview; pressure to decide quickly; messages from personal email addresses or only through social media; poor spelling; and requests for your bank details, passport or TRN before a real offer. Overseas work is a common trap, with promises of hotel jobs abroad. To stay safe, I would research the company and check that its address and phone number are real. I would check that any recruitment agency is licensed with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, and get information about overseas work only from the Ministry's official programmes or from well-known employers. I would never pay to be given a job, never send my passport or documents to someone I have not checked, and talk it over with my instructor or family first. If I find a scam, I would report it to the police and warn others.
markingPoints: Explains what a job scam is (it takes money or personal details)
Gives at least three warning signs
Mentions overseas job offers as a common trap
Checks the company and that agencies are licensed; uses official overseas programmes
Never pays for a job or sends documents unchecked; asks for advice and reports scams

essays.stem: Describe how to write a CV and a cover letter for a hotel job, and what each should include.
essays.modelAnswer: A CV should be short, clear and neat, usually one or two pages, typed in a plain font, with no spelling mistakes. At the top I put my full name, phone number, a professional email address and the area I live in. Next I write a short profile of two or three lines, for example: "Trained room attendant with NVQ-J Level 2, friendly and reliable, seeking a housekeeping position in a resort." Then I list my education and training, starting with the most recent, including my NVQ-J certificate and Food Handler's Permit. After that I list my work experience, including work attachments and part-time jobs, with dates and the main duties. I add my key skills, such as making beds to hotel standard, customer service and teamwork, and any languages. Last, I give two referees, after asking their permission. With the CV I send a short cover letter that names the job, says why I want it and how my skills match it, and asks for an interview. I change both for each job I apply for.
markingPoints: CV is short, clear and neat, and checked for mistakes
Contact details with a professional email, and a short profile
Education and training (most recent first), and work experience with duties
Key skills, and referees given with their permission
A cover letter matched to the job, and both changed for each application

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare for a job interview at a hotel or villa, and how to behave on the day.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the interview, I would research the hotel or villa: where it is, the type of guests it serves and what it is known for. I would read the job advert again and think about how my skills match it. I would practise answers to common questions, such as "Tell me about yourself", "Why do you want to work here?" and "How would you deal with an unhappy guest?", using real examples from my training. I would prepare two questions to ask, such as what training new staff receive. I would get my documents ready, such as copies of my CV, certificates and Food Handler's Permit, and plan my travel so that I arrive 10 to 15 minutes early. On the day, I would dress neatly and simply, be well groomed, and switch my phone to silent. I would greet everyone politely, shake hands if offered, sit up straight, make eye contact and smile. I would listen carefully, answer clearly and honestly, and never speak badly of a past employer. At the end, I would thank the interviewer, and afterwards send a short thank-you message.
markingPoints: Researches the employer and reads the advert again
Practises answers to common questions with real examples, and prepares questions to ask
Gets documents ready and plans to arrive 10 to 15 minutes early
On the day: neat appearance, phone on silent, a polite greeting and good body language
Answers clearly and honestly, thanks the interviewer, and follows up with a thank-you message

essays.stem: Explain how to set SMART goals for your job search, and give an example plan with steps and dates.
essays.modelAnswer: A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. A vague goal like "get a good job" is hard to act on, but a SMART goal gives me a clear target and a deadline, so that I can plan the steps and check my progress. For example, my goal could be: "By the end of March, I will have a job as a room attendant at a hotel or villa on the north coast." To reach it, I would set smaller steps with dates. In week 1, I will update my CV and make copies of my certificates and Food Handler's Permit. In week 2, I will ask two instructors to be my referees and tell my contacts that I am looking for work. Each week, I will check job sites, newspapers and hotel social media pages, and apply for at least three suitable jobs. I will keep a log of every application and follow up after one week. I will practise interview answers with a classmate. At the end of each month, I will review my progress and change the plan if needed.
markingPoints: Explains each part of SMART
Explains why SMART goals help (a clear target, a deadline, progress can be checked)
Gives a correct SMART job goal
Breaks it into steps with dates
Includes tracking and a regular review of the plan

essays.stem: Explain how to keep a job search going: tracking applications, following up, and dealing with rejection.
essays.modelAnswer: A job search can take weeks or months, so it needs a plan. I would keep a job search log, on paper or on my phone, listing each job I apply for, the employer, the date, how I applied, the contact person and what happens next. This stops me missing closing dates or forgetting who I spoke to. If I hear nothing after about one or two weeks, I would follow up politely by phone or email, to check that my application was received and to show that I am keen. After an interview, I would send a thank-you message. If I am turned down, I would not take it personally, because many people apply for each job. I would thank the employer, ask politely for feedback, and use it to improve my CV or my interview answers. I would keep applying, set small weekly targets, and look after myself by keeping a routine, exercising and talking to supportive people. While I search, I can keep learning, volunteer or take short-term work, which builds my skills and my contacts.
markingPoints: Keeps a job search log with useful details
Follows up applications politely after a set time
Deals with rejection calmly and asks for feedback
Uses the feedback to improve, and keeps applying with weekly targets
Stays positive with a routine and support, and keeps learning, volunteering or taking short-term work

practical1.title: Find and analyse hospitality job opportunities, and make a job search plan
practical1.brief: As a group, find and analyse real or sample job opportunities in hotels, villas and other tourism businesses, then make a job search plan. Using the Centre's computers or training devices (or your own phone only if you agree), each member finds at least two job adverts from different sources, for example an online job site, a hotel's own website or social media page, a newspaper, and the Centre's job board, and fills in a job advert analysis sheet for each: job title, employer, location, duties, essential and desirable requirements, closing date, how to apply, and whether the job matches their own skills. Each member also checks one advert for scam warning signs. Together, make a chart of the sources you used, with one strength and one weakness of each, and set up a job search log for the group. Finally, each member writes a SMART job goal and a 4-week plan with steps and dates. Do not log in to personal accounts or show personal details in the photos. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the analysis sheets, the chart, the log and the plans once for the whole group.
materials: The Centre's computers or training devices with internet access
Newspapers with job adverts, and the Centre's job board
Job advert analysis sheets, a scam warning-sign checklist and a job search log sheet
Blank SMART goal and 4-week plan sheets
photos: Each member searching a different source on screen or in a newspaper (one photo per member, no personal details showing)
The completed job advert analysis sheets
The scam warning-sign check on one advert
The chart of sources with their strengths and weaknesses
Each member's SMART goal and 4-week plan
checklist: Found at least two suitable job adverts from different sources
Recorded the duties, essential and desirable requirements, closing date and how to apply correctly
Judged sensibly whether each job matched their own skills
Checked an advert for scam warning signs correctly
Gave a sensible strength and weakness for a source on the group chart
Wrote a SMART job goal with a realistic 4-week plan
Kept personal details private while using the devices
safety: Use only the Centre's devices and practice accounts, or your own phone only if you agree
Do not enter personal details, passwords or bank details on any job site during the task
Do not reply to or click links in suspicious job messages; show them to the assessor
Sit with a straight back and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Prepare a CV and cover letter, and practise a job enquiry call and an interview
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare applications and practise contacting an employer and being interviewed. Part 1: each member writes a one-page CV and a short cover letter for one hotel or villa job advert, either from Practical 1 or one the assessor gives. A member may use a made-up address and phone number if they prefer. Another member checks each CV and letter against a checklist and suggests improvements, and the writer makes the changes. Part 2: in pairs, act out a phone enquiry to a villa company asking about job openings, with a polite greeting, a short summary of what you offer and a clear question. Part 3: each member is interviewed for their chosen job for about 10 minutes by another member (or the assessor) using a list of common interview questions, while a third member fills in a score sheet on appearance, body language, answers and questions asked. Part 4: each member drafts a short thank-you message after the interview. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the written work to the group's practical.
materials: Job adverts from Practical 1 or from the assessor
The Centre's computers and printer, or paper and pens
A CV and cover letter checklist
Two phones or a desk and phone for the enquiry call
A table and chairs set up as an interview room, a list of interview questions and score sheets
photos: Each member's first draft CV and cover letter (personal details covered if wanted)
The peer check, with the checklist filled in
The final CVs and cover letters
Each member's interview (one photo per member)
The completed score sheets and the thank-you messages
checklist: Wrote a clear, neat, one-page CV with the right sections and no spelling mistakes
Wrote a cover letter matched to the job, saying why they want it and how they fit
Checked another member's CV and gave helpful suggestions, and improved their own
Made a polite, clear phone enquiry
Was neatly presented and used good body language in the interview
Answered interview questions clearly, with examples, and asked a sensible question
safety: Members may use a made-up address and phone number; do not share real personal details beyond the group and the assessor
Do not post the CVs or the photos online
Keep the role plays calm and polite
Keep cables from the computers and printer out of walkways
